# Class 12 semiconductors, ~2 minutes, written by Claude for F-014 S4 (hard topics). Expect: a content slide on doping;
# "the road junction" and "depletion of the ozone layer" are traps; "let me show you a p-n junction" opens simulation
# mode (nothing printed yet); both sides doped at 10^16 per cubic centimetre: V_bi 0.714 V, W 430 nm (no bias, absent
# = known), E_max 33.2 kV/cm; reverse bias of 5 V: W 1.22 µm; "increase it to 10 volts" stays reverse (W 1.66 µm);
# the Zener line is a notice; then forward 0.6 V with I_s 10^-12 A: I = 12 mA, W 172 nm; back to the slides.
@setup subject=Physics grade=12 topic="Semiconductor devices"

Good morning. Today we study what happens where p-type and n-type silicon meet.
[pause 1]
A p-type crystal is doped with acceptors, so it has extra holes, and an n-type crystal is doped with donors.
Think of it like the road junction near the school, where two streams of traffic meet.
The depletion of the ozone layer is a different story for another day.
[pause 1.5]
Let me show you a p-n junction.
Both sides are doped at ten to the power sixteen per cubic centimetre, and there is no bias yet.
[pause 1]
Electrons diffuse from the n side and holes from the p side, leaving fixed ions behind.
These ions set up an electric field which stops further diffusion.
[pause 1]
Now apply a reverse bias of 5 volts.
See how the depletion region becomes wider.
Now increase it to 10 volts.
A Zener diode would break down at a high reverse voltage, but our diode does not.
[pause 1.5]
Now apply a forward bias of 0.6 volts instead.
The saturation current is 10 to the power minus 12 amperes.
The depletion region becomes narrow, and a large current flows.
[pause 1.5]
Okay, let's get back to the slides.
[pause 1]
So a diode conducts in forward bias and blocks in reverse bias.
